messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 20
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Writer
- Trauma Type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
- Pcl5: 72

Rain drums against the street below. Ravi is supposed to meet his younger brother, Samir, from the university library. A text pings on his phone: “Running late. Don’t wait.” The screen goes dark. By the time Ravi grabs his keys, the sirens have already started, a continuous, rising wail that doesn’t stop. Glass. Then silence. Then the hospital waiting room, then the funeral hall, then the neighborhood women pouring turmeric water at the gate while his father stands perfectly still. The timeline fractures. Days blur into a single, endless stretch. He stops counting the hours after the first week. He only counts the distance between safety and the intersection. The mourning ends. Ravi does not. At twenty, he lives alone in a third-floor walk-up. His mother sends him packages of spices he cannot cook. His friends text invitations to the arcade, to a weekend train ride, to a new gallery opening. He reads them and replies, “Can’t make it. Working.” He is not working. He is sitting on the floor, sorting a stack of Samir’s notebooks. Each page contains the same sentence, rewritten forty times, each version failing to capture the exact shade of the afternoon sky before the intersection. Writing used to be a river. Now it is a room with locked doors. He sits at his desk, fingers hovering above the keyboard. When he types, the words feel heavy, like stones dragged through water. He deletes a paragraph. He types it again. He checks the timestamp on every email. A dropped pen sounds like shattering glass. His heart hammers against his ribs, and he waits for the ceiling to stop vibrating. He hasn’t driven in eleven months. He rides the bus, sitting in the very back row, eyes fixed on the cracked leather in front of him. At night, the rumble of a distant engine wakes him instantly. He counts the tires on passing cars. He checks the deadbolt three times, walks to the window, checks it again. His body stays coiled, ready for a collision that already happened. He tells himself he is permanently broken. He stops believing his own judgment. When his freelance publisher calls, he lets it go to voicemail. He tells himself he will respond tomorrow. He has told himself this for forty-seven days. The blank document stares back, demanding a deadline he cannot meet. He exports a draft, reads it aloud to himself, then deletes the entire file. He starts over. The guilt doesn’t shout; it settles. He traces the edge of his keyboard until his fingers ache, mapping the ridges like blind fingers. Every notification is a phantom. Every car that slows down near his building makes his breath catch. He waits for the knock, the phone call, the end. It never comes. The silence stretches, heavy and absolute. The apartment smells like stale coffee and old paper. He keeps the blinds drawn until noon. When he finally opens them, he watches the street. A siren wails, far away, moving on. He doesn’t flinch. He stands at the sink, washing a single mug. The water runs cold. He watches the soap swirl down the drain. Then he turns off the tap, dries his hands, and walks back to the desk. The cursor blinks. He exhales, long and slow, and lets his fingers find the keys. He pauses, listening to the quiet. It is the same quiet that followed the impact. He waits for the next sound, the next shift in the air. It doesn’t come. He settles into the chair, shoulders dropping a fraction. He begins to type.
